opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the starting point was really understanding what earlier state space models like S4 were good at and where they fell short. Those models were linear time-invariant: the parameters governing how the hidden state evolves are the same at every time step, no matter what the input is. That's exactly what made them efficient, because you can unroll the recurrence into one big convolution and compute it in parallel with FFTs. But it also means the model can't decide, based on content, what to remember and what to ignore. We looked at synthetic tasks like selective copying and induction heads, and those models struggled precisely because they couldn't filter information based on what they were seeing.

So the core idea in Mamba was simple to state: make some of the SSM parameters functions of the input. Specifically, the step size delta and the B and C matrices are computed from the current token. Delta is the most interesting one. It acts like a gate. A large delta means "focus on this input and reset the state," and a small delta means "mostly ignore this and keep what you have." That connects to classical gating in RNNs like LSTMs and GRUs, which was a nice conceptual link.

The catch is that once the parameters vary with time, you lose the convolution trick, so you're back to a recurrence. Naively, a recurrence is sequential and slow, and materializing that expanded hidden state for every time step costs a lot of memory. That's where the hardware-aware part came in, and Tri Dao's expertise was essential there.

There were a few pieces. First, even though it's a recurrence, it's a linear one, so you can compute it with a parallel scan instead of a strictly sequential loop. Second, and more important in practice, we were careful about the GPU memory hierarchy. The big expanded state never gets written out to the GPU's main high-bandwidth memory. We load the parameters into fast on-chip SRAM, do the discretization and the scan there, and write back only the final outputs, which are much smaller. That's very much in the spirit of FlashAttention, where the bottleneck is memory movement rather than raw compute. Third, for the backward pass we use recomputation: instead of storing intermediate states, we recompute them, which keeps memory usage comparable to an optimized attention implementation.

Put together, you get a model that scales linearly in sequence length, has constant-time per-step inference like an RNN since there's no growing KV cache, and still has the content-dependent reasoning that made attention so effective. The broader lesson for me was that you can't design the algorithm and the hardware implementation separately. The selectivity idea only became practical because we co-designed it with how GPUs actually work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the starting point was this realization that the thing that made S4 and the earlier structured state space models so efficient was also what was holding them back. Those models are linear time-invariant. The A, B, and C matrices that govern the recurrence are fixed. They don't depend on the input at all. And that's great computationally, because when your dynamics are constant you can unroll the whole recurrence into a single global convolution and compute it with FFTs. But it means the model literally cannot do input-dependent reasoning. It can't look at a token and decide, "this one matters, remember it," or "this one is noise, forget it." We built these little synthetic tasks, selective copying and induction heads, and the LTI models just fail on them, because they have no mechanism for content-based selection. Attention, of course, does this trivially. That's kind of its whole thing.

So the first move was conceptually simple: make the parameters functions of the input. The B matrix, the C matrix, and especially the step size delta all become projections of the current token. Delta turned out to be the really important one. If you think of it as a gate on the recurrence, a large delta means "reset the state and pay attention to this input," a small delta means "ignore this and keep what you had." That connects back to gating in RNNs, and you can actually derive classic gating mechanisms as special cases of this discretization. So selectivity was really about giving the model a time-varying recurrence.

The problem is that the moment you do that, you lose the convolution. There's no longer a single kernel to compute. And a naive recurrence on a GPU is terrible, because you're materializing this large hidden state, in our case something like sixteen times the model dimension, at every time step, and shuttling it back and forth to HBM. You're completely memory-bandwidth bound.

So the second half of the work was really a systems problem. The main idea was to be hardware-aware about where the state lives. We don't ever write the expanded state out to main GPU memory. We load the inputs into SRAM, do the discretization and the scan there, and only write back the outputs, which are the small model dimension. So the big tensor only ever exists in fast on-chip memory. The scan itself we do as a parallel associative scan, which is a well-known primitive, but fusing it with the discretization into one kernel is what makes it work. And then for the backward pass we recompute the intermediate states rather than storing them, which is the same trick FlashAttention uses. It costs you some FLOPs but FLOPs are cheap relative to memory traffic.

The end result is that you get something that in practice runs as fast or faster than the convolutional S4 models and significantly faster than FlashAttention at longer sequence lengths, with constant memory per token during inference because you're just carrying a fixed-size state forward. And then the last piece was simplifying the architecture, collapsing the separate SSM block and the gated MLP into one homogeneous block, which is what became the Mamba block. But honestly, the core insight was just: the thing that looked like a constraint, this time-invariance, was actually a modeling limitation, and the price of removing it was a kernel-engineering problem rather than a fundamental one.

astra-6.text:
The key idea was to let the model decide what to remember based on the input. In a traditional state space model, the dynamics are fixed: you apply the same update rule regardless of what token you’re seeing. That structure is useful computationally, but it makes it difficult to selectively retain important information and ignore distractions.

So we made parts of the state update depend on the current input. The challenge is that you lose the fixed convolution that made earlier state space models efficient. We needed a different way to compute the sequence.

We approached that with a hardware-aware parallel scan. Although the model is recurrent, these updates have structure that lets you compute them in parallel during training. And we organized the computation to avoid writing the large intermediate states to GPU memory, doing as much work as possible in the faster on-chip memory. We also recompute intermediate states during the backward pass rather than storing all of them.

So there are really two pieces: input-dependent dynamics give you selectivity, and the GPU implementation makes that selectivity practical. At inference time, you still have a recurrent update with a fixed-size state.

sol-6.1.text:
The starting point was to ask what we were giving up to make state space models efficient. In the earlier models, the dynamics were fixed regardless of the input. That structure lets you compute them very efficiently as convolutions, but it also makes it difficult to decide which information to remember and which information to ignore.

So we made parts of the model input dependent. You can think of that as allowing the model to selectively write information into its state, retain it, or forget it. The challenge is that once you do that, you lose the convolutional formulation that made those earlier models fast.

Our approach was to use a parallel scan and design the implementation around the GPU’s memory hierarchy. Rather than materializing the entire expanded state in GPU memory, we keep the intermediate computation in faster memory and fuse the operations together. That gives us input-dependent selection while preserving efficient training and linear scaling with sequence length. At inference time, you still have a recurrent model with a fixed-size state.
